label: theorem:inversion
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{theorem:inversion}
Let $\Lambda \in \Lambda(n)$ and $\mathbf{r} = (r_1,\dotsc,r_n) \in \mathcal{H}_n$. There exist a unique 
$R\in R'(n)$ whose first row is $\mathbf{r}$ and a unique $T\in \mathcal{T}'(n)$  
such that $T = R\Lambda R^{-1}$, except for $\mathbf{r}$ belonging to an exceptional set $M\subset \mathcal{H}_n$
of measure zero.

title: Proof
body_md:
One can prove by induction that
\[
\mathbf{e}_k^t\widetilde{T}^j\mathbf{e}_1= \begin{cases} \widetilde{b}_{n-1}\widetilde{b}_{n-2}\dotsm \widetilde{b}_{n-j}, & \text{if $k=j+1$,}\\
0, & \text{if $k>j+1$.} \end{cases}  
\]
It follows that for any $\psi \in \mathcal{P}_j[\mathbb{C}]$ we have
\[
\bigl \|\psi(\widetilde{T})\mathbf{e}_1\bigr \| \ge \bigl |\widetilde{b}_{n-1}\widetilde{b}_{n-2}\dotsm \widetilde{b}_{n-j}\bigr |. 
\]
This lower bound is sharp if there exist a $\psi\in \mathcal{P}_j[\mathbb{C}]$ such that
\[
\psi(\widetilde{T})\mathbf{e}_1 = \mathbf{e}_{j+1}\widetilde{b}_{n-1}\widetilde{b}_{n-2}\dotsm \widetilde{b}_{n-j}.
\]

Note that the first $j$ components of $\widetilde{T}^j\mathbf{e}_1$ contain  only elements 
from $\widetilde{T}_j$, as do the vectors $\widetilde{T}^k\mathbf{e}_1$ for $1\le k<j$. 
Let 
\[
E_j=(\mathbf{e}_1,\dotsc ,\mathbf{e}_j).
\]
Then, we have
\[
E_j^t\psi(\widetilde{T})\mathbf{e}_1 = \psi(\widetilde{T}_j)\mathbf{e}_1,
\]
where, with an abuse of notation, $\mathbf{e}_1$ on the left-hand
side belongs to ${\mathbb C}^n$, while on the right-hand side $\mathbf{e}_1\in {\mathbb C}^j$.  
The Cayley-Hamilton theorem states that $\chi_j(\widetilde{T}_j)=0$. 
It follows that
\[
\chi_j(\widetilde{T})\mathbf{e}_1 = \mathbf{e}_{j+1}\widetilde{b}_{n-1}\widetilde{b}_{n-2}\dotsm \widetilde{b}_{n-j}.
\]
This proves statements 1. and 2.  The proof of 3. and 4. is analogous.

label: lem:jac1
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:jac1}
Let $T=R\Lambda R^{-1}$ be the spectral decomposition of $T\in \mathcal{T}(n)$, where $R$ is defined in~\eqref{eq:newnot} and
$\Lambda = \operatorname{diag}(\lambda_1, \dotsc,\lambda_n)$. We have
\[
\Delta(\boldsymbol{\lambda})^2=\frac{\prod_{j=1}^{n-1}b_j^j}{\prod_{j=1}^{n}r_{j}},
\]
where $\mathbf{r} = (r_1,\dotsc,r_n)$ is the first row of $R$ and
\[
r_1 + \dotsb + r_n =1.
\]
